note: Said in advance: predictions about AI, each quoted word for word from where it was made, with the year it named and what the record shows happened. Every `words` and every evidence `quote` is verbatim from the source named beside it. A verdict is about the words, not the person.

predictions.title: A machine fools an average interrogator, in about fifty years
predictions.words: I believe that in about fifty years' time it will be possible to programme computers, with a storage capacity of about 10⁹, to make them play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 per cent. chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning.
predictions.short: Turing wrote in 1950 that in about fifty years an average interrogator would be right no more than 70 per cent of the time after five minutes with a machine. In a 2025 test GPT-4.5 was taken for the human 73 per cent of the time.
reading: Turing's figure is exact enough to check: an average interrogator right no more than 70 per cent of the time after five minutes of questioning — the machine taken for the human at least three times in ten. His fifty years ran to 2000.

In 2025 Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen ran three-party tests on Turing's own terms, five-minute conversations with a person and a machine at once. Prompted to adopt a humanlike persona, GPT-4.5 was picked as the human 73 per cent of the time, more often than the real person. On that measure the prediction came true, twenty-five years late; the board's card files it as passed, by one measure.

evidence.quote: When prompted to adopt a humanlike persona, GPT-4.5 was judged to be the human 73% of the time: significantly more often than interrogators selected the real human participant.
Participants had 5 minute conversations simultaneously with another human participant and one of these systems before judging which conversational partner they thought was human.
The results constitute the first empirical evidence that any artificial system passes a standard three-party Turing test.

sources.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
Large Language Models Pass the Turing Test

record.note: The card files the prediction, and the 2025 result as passed by one measure.

predictions.open: Whether an earlier claim, on looser terms, met the line first is not settled here. The board scores the 2025 study, which its authors call the first evidence of any system passing a standard three-party test.

predictions.title: A significant advance on thinking machines, from one summer's work
predictions.who: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon
predictions.words: We think that a significant advance can be made in one or more of these problems if a carefully selected group of scientists work on it together for a summer.
predictions.short: The 1955 proposal that named the field said a significant advance could be made if a chosen group worked on it together for a summer. In 1956, McCarthy wrote later, there was no real joint work; the first result he traced to the summer came in 1959.
reading: The proposal, dated 31 August 1955, set its own terms: a carefully selected group, working together, for a summer. In 1987 McCarthy wrote that some invitees did not come at all and most came for short stays that did not overlap. There was no real joint work, and the direct scientific result was meagre. On its own terms the summer's promise was never tested, and not kept.

Read as a promise that the problems would yield to a concerted attack, it came true late. McCarthy traced one line from the summer to IBM: Herbert Gelernter, who started work in September 1956, had a geometry theorem prover by 1959. The board scores it on that reading, and keeps the other beside it.

evidence.quote: In the event, some invitees didn't come at all and almost all came for short periods, not all overlapping. There was no real joint work.
In spite of this meager direct scientific result, though perhaps no more meager than that of many conferences, I believe it played an important role in the future of AI.

Rochester decided to take it up, and a new Ph.D. in physics, Herbert Gelernter, who started work in September 1956 took up the project and produced a geometry theorem prover by 1959, IBM's best AI work so far.

predictions.title: A computer becomes the world's chess champion within ten years
predictions.words: That within ten years a digital computer will be the world's chess champion, unless the rules bar it from competition.
predictions.short: Simon and Newell said in November 1957 that within ten years a computer would be the world's chess champion, unless the rules barred it from competition. Deep Blue beat the reigning champion in a match in 1997, thirty years late.
reading: The first of four predictions Simon made in an address on 14 November 1957, printed with Newell two months later: within ten years a computer would be chess champion, discover and prove an important new theorem, write music critics would accept, and turn most theories in psychology into programs. The theorem is filed here too; the music and the psychology are not, because no card on the board can settle them.

Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov, the reigning champion, in a match in May 1997, thirty years after the deadline. Read word for word it never came: no computer has held the title, which is the case Simon's own clause, unless the rules bar it, allowed for. Minsky said so in 1997; Simon, the next year, called the predictions a highly successful exercise in futurology that he would make again.

evidence.quote: In May of that year, it became the first computer system to defeat a reigning world chess champion in a match under standard tournament controls.
Herbert Simon said in 1958 that a program would be chess champion in ten years, and, as we know, the IBM group has done extremely well, but even now [Deep Blue] is not the undisputed champion.

Just for your own information, (a) I regard the predictions as a highly successful exercise in futurology, and (b) placed in the equivalent position today, I would make them again, and for the same reasons. (Some people never seem to learn.)

predictions.title: A computer discovers and proves an important new theorem within ten years
predictions.words: That within ten years a digital computer will discover and prove an important new mathematical theorem.
predictions.short: The second of Simon and Newell's four: within ten years a computer would discover and prove an important new theorem. On a loose reading it came in 1976; on the strict one, in 2026, when a model disproved an Erdős conjecture that experts called important.
reading: Dreyfus wrote in 1965 that the field was still a long way from the important theorem promised for 1967. In 1976 a computer checked the cases of the four-colour theorem — the first major theorem proved with one, but a conjecture from 1852 and a proof its human authors designed.

In May 2026 an internal OpenAI model disproved Erdős's eighty-year-old conjecture on unit distances. Scientific American wrote that the result would merit a top journal even if people had done it alone, and Timothy Gowers that no earlier machine proof had come close; a mathematician quoted in the same article said very similar ideas in the literature had not been credited. The board scores the strict reading: came, sixty years late.

predictions.title: No computer chess champion by Simon's deadline of 1967
predictions.words: Still no chess program can play even amateur chess, and the world championship tournament is only two years away.
predictions.short: Dreyfus wrote in 1965 that still no chess program can play even amateur chess, and that Simon's world championship was only two years away. No computer was champion in 1967 — but that year a program at MIT beat Dreyfus.
reading: The sentence describes the present and mocks a deadline; it forecasts only that Simon's would pass, and it did. The description did not last the two years: in 1967 Richard Greenblatt's chess program beat Dreyfus at MIT, and SIGART reprinted the game with one phrase from his paper.

Dreyfus replied, in Seymour Papert's account, that he had been making a statement of fact, not a prediction. The version usually quoted — no program could play even amateur chess — is a later retelling, printed in quotation marks in a 2010 history of the field. The paper says can.

evidence.quote: chess program at M.I.T. and seeing him very roundly trounced. The newsletter SIGART reprinted the game with no comment beyond one phrase from Alchemy: "... no chess program can play even amateur chess." (p. 10)
Dreyfus indignantly replied that he was being misquoted: he was making a statement of fact, not a prediction.
Dreyfus said, oh, sure. And sure enough, Dreyfus sat down and got beat.
Greenblatt’s program beat Hubert Dreyfus (1929– ), an AI critic who had earlier observed that “no chess program could play even amateur chess.”

predictions.title: Machines capable of any work a man can do, within twenty years
predictions.words: Technologically, as I have argued earlier, machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work that a man can do.
predictions.short: Simon wrote in 1960 that machines would be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work that a man can do. It is usually quoted from his 1965 reprint, and without the 'that'. The twenty years ran out in 1980.
reading: The line is from the third of Simon's 1960 lectures, The New Science of Management Decision, and was reprinted in The Shape of Automation for Men and Management in 1965 — which is why it is usually dated 1965 and given a deadline of 1985. Either way it has passed.

His next sentence keeps for people their greatest comparative advantage in jobs that need flexible handling of a rough environment: he forecast what machines could technically do, not that they would do it. Nothing on the record says any work at all can yet be done by a machine; the 2026 argument is over general intelligence, hedged and disputed the day it was made.

evidence.quote: In 1960 Herbert A. Simon published “The New Science of Management Decision”, and he did assert that computer systems would achieve extraordinarily broad capabilities within two decades, i.e., by 1980.
The chapter containing the quotation under examination was reprinted in Simon’s 1965 book “The Shape of Automation for Men and Management”.
Economically, men will retain their greatest comparative advantage in jobs that require flexible manipulation of those parts of the environment that are relatively rough

predictions.short: Kurzweil wrote in 1990 that a computer world chess champion was a reasonable expectation by the end of the century. Deep Blue beat the reigning champion in a match in May 1997, three years inside his date.
reading: The sentence is from the chess chapter of The Age of Intelligent Machines, as Kurzweil's company put it on the web in 1996; the book's chronology dates the same event to 2000. The 1998 often attached to it is his own later arithmetic: in 2002 he wrote that his estimate of the machines' gain in rating points a year had put the cross-over at 1998.

Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov, the reigning world champion, in a six-game match in New York in May 1997. Read as Kurzweil read it — a computer beating the champion — it came true early. Read word for word, no computer has ever held the title.

predictions.title: No computer passes the Turing test by the end of 2029, under a bet’s rules
predictions.who: Mitchell Kapor, betting against Ray Kurzweil
predictions.words: By 2029 no computer - or "machine intelligence" - will have passed the Turing Test.
predictions.short: In 2002 Mitchell Kapor bet Ray Kurzweil $20,000 that no computer would pass the Turing test by the end of 2029, under rules of two-hour interviews by three judges. A 2025 study reported a pass in five-minute chats; under the bet's rules, none yet.
reading: The sentence is Kapor's side of the first wager on Long Bets. If a computer passes before the end of 2029, Kurzweil wins; otherwise Kapor does. The rules are strict: each of three judges interviews the computer and three human foils for two hours, and the computer must fool two of the three judges and rank as human as two of the foils.

In 2025 Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen reported the first evidence that an artificial system passes a standard three-party Turing test — in five-minute conversations. Nothing on the record has been run under the bet's rules, and its year has not come.

evidence.quote: If a Computer passes the Turing Test, as described above, prior to the end of the year 2029, then Ray Kurzweil wins the wager. Otherwise Mitchell Kapor wins the wager.
The Computer will be deemed to have passed the "Turing Test Human Determination Test" if the Computer has fooled two or more of the three Human Judges into thinking that it is a human.
STAKES $20,000 will go to The Electronic Frontier Foundation if Kapor wins, or The Kurzweil Foundation if Kurzweil wins.
Participants had 5 minute conversations simultaneously with another human participant and one of these systems before judging which conversational partner they thought was human.
The results constitute the first empirical evidence that any artificial system passes a standard three-party Turing test.

DeepMind's AlphaGo beat the European champion Fan Hui 5–0 in October 2015, and Nature's paper the next January called it a feat previously thought to be at least a decade away. The forecast erred towards caution, which is the board's reading of Go: since then, estimates of what is hard have not been trusted in either direction.

predictions.title: Seven to ten GPT-4-level models, and no massive advance, by the end of 2024
predictions.words: Prediction: By end of 2024 we will see • 7-10 GPT-4 level models • No massive advance (no GPT-5, or disappointing GPT-5)
predictions.short: Marcus predicted in March 2024 that the year would bring seven to ten GPT-4-level models and no massive advance — no GPT-5, or a disappointing one. GPT-5 came in August 2025. Whether the rest held is argued.
reading: The GPT-5 clause is clean: OpenAI introduced GPT-5 in August 2025, and none arrived in 2024. On 1 January 2025 Marcus scored his seven predictions for the year as all right, with a possible asterisk for OpenAI's o3.

A critic, scoring them at Marcus's invitation, counted more than twenty GPT-4-level models from over ten companies, and called 'no massive advance' false, pointing to OpenAI's reasoning models. Whether the parenthesis — no GPT-5 — defines a massive advance or only gives an example of one decides the verdict.

evidence.quote: We are introducing GPT‑5, our best AI system yet.
The top AI moment of 2024 was not the much-anticipated release of GPT-5, which never arrived, even though fans kept predicting it, all year long.
With a possible asterisk on OpenAI’s o3, which was announced in December but not released or exposed to broad scrutiny, all seven were pretty much right on the money.
Counting these models, I get 20+ models at GPT-4 level (from over 10 distinct companies).
No massive advance: False, unless I am missing some definition that makes this true.

predictions.title: AI does well on every test you can list within five years
predictions.words: If I gave an AI ... every single test that you can possibly imagine, you make that list of tests and put it in front of the computer science industry, and I'm guessing in five years time, we'll do well on every single one
predictions.short: At Stanford in March 2024 Huang guessed that within five years AI would do well on every test you could put in front of it. In September 2026 he wrote that AGI had arrived. The year he named is 2029.
reading: Reuters reported the answer as a definition of general intelligence: if it means passing tests, Huang said, it is near. Stanford's own account of the talk read it as every test a human takes, specialised medical licensing exams included.

Two and a half years on, the board's benchmark cards show tests still not passed on standard terms, and others built to last years saturated within months. Huang's 2026 'AGI has arrived' was a claim about general intelligence, not about every test.

evidence.quote: Huang predicted that in as little as five years AI will be able to pass every test a human takes — not just the legal bar exams that it can complete today, but also highly specialized medical licensing exams.
Jensen Huang, CEO of chipmaker Nvidia – a major partner of OpenAI – added his thoughts on Monday, writing on social media that “AGI has arrived” with Astra’s release.

predictions.title: The first AI agents join the workforce in 2025
predictions.words: We are now confident we know how to build AGI as we have traditionally understood it. We believe that, in 2025, we may see the first AI agents “join the workforce” and materially change the output of companies.
predictions.short: Altman wrote in January 2025 that the first AI agents might join the workforce that year and materially change the output of companies. By June he said they had arrived. Surveys and a controlled study that summer said otherwise.
reading: The claim is hedged — 'we may see' — and the sentence before it, that OpenAI knew how to build AGI, names no date and is not scored. In June 2025 Altman wrote that the year had seen agents that do real cognitive work, and that writing code would never be the same; the board's 2025 card agrees for software.

Against it: in Stack Overflow's survey that summer most developers did not use agents, a report from MIT found 95 per cent of organisations getting no return on generative AI, and a controlled study by METR found experienced developers slower with AI tools, not faster. Whether agents changed the output of companies in 2025 is the dispute.

evidence.quote: 2025 has seen the arrival of agents that can do real cognitive work; writing computer code will never be the same.
AI agents are not yet mainstream. A majority of developers (52%) either don't use agents or stick to simpler AI tools, and a significant portion (38%) have no plans to adopt them.
Despite $30–40 billion in enterprise investment into GenAI, this report uncovers a surprising result in that 95% of organizations are getting zero return.
Surprisingly, we find that when developers use AI tools, they take 19% longer than without—AI makes them slower.

predictions.title: AI writes 90 per cent of the code within three to six months
predictions.words: what we are finding is we are not far from the world—I think we’ll be there in three to six months—where AI is writing 90 percent of the code. And then in twelve months, we may be in a world where AI is writing essentially all of the code.
predictions.short: Amodei said in March 2025 that within three to six months AI would be writing 90 per cent of the code. Inside Anthropic, by its own conservative count, more than 80 per cent of merged code was Claude's by May 2026. Across the industry, less.
reading: As said, about code in general, it did not happen on time: Google, counting its own, reported nearly half of new code written by AI in October 2025 and 75 per cent in April 2026, and an independent study of open-source code put the American share at about 29 per cent at the end of 2024.

As Amodei later defended it — inside Anthropic and some of its customers — he called it absolutely true in October 2025, then added, not uniformly. Anthropic's own count, published in June 2026, put Claude's share of merged code above 80 per cent by May, while its leadership's estimate, scripts included, was 90 per cent or more. The two readings give two verdicts.

evidence.quote: Some people think that prediction is wrong, but within Anthropic and within a number of companies that we work with, that is absolutely true.
As of May 2026, more than 80% of the code we merge into Anthropic’s codebase was authored by Claude.

Anthropic leadership have publicly estimated that 90% or more of our code is written by Claude, including scripts and experimental code. Our >80% figure measures the share of lines merged to production that can be attributed to Claude.
Today, nearly half of all new code at Google is generated by AI, reviewed and accepted by engineers.
Today, 75% of all new code at Google is now AI-generated and approved by engineers, up from 50% last fall.
About 29% of Python functions in the US were generated by AI by the end of 2024, closely followed by 23/24% for Germany and France.

predictions.title: AI smarter than any one human, around the end of 2025
predictions.words: My guess is that we’ll have AI that is smarter than any one human probably around the end of next year
predictions.byWords: around the end of next year
predictions.short: Musk said in April 2024 that he guessed AI would be smarter than any one human around the end of 2025. At Davos in January 2026 he moved it to the end of 2026, and no later than 2027.
reading: No transcript of the interview has been found, and the two reports of it differ: The Guardian has 'around the end of next year', Reuters 'probably next year, within two years'. On the first the year has passed; on the second, 2026 is still running.

Musk's own later words put it ahead both times. At Davos in January 2026 he said it might happen by the end of that year, and no later than the next; at his trial against OpenAI's leaders in May he said 'we are getting close to that point'. Nothing on the record says it has happened.

evidence.quote: If you define AGI (artificial general intelligence) as smarter than the smartest human, I think it's probably next year, within two years
The rate at which AI is progressing, I think we might have AI that is smarter than any human by the end of this year, and I would say no later than next year

Asked to describe artificial general intelligence, Musk said it is when AI becomes "as smart as any human," and added that "we are getting close to that point," and AI will be smarter than any human as soon as next year.

predictions.title: Powerful AI could come as early as 2026
predictions.words: I think it could come as early as 2026, though there are also ways it could take much longer.
predictions.short: Amodei wrote in October 2024 that powerful AI — smarter than a Nobel laureate across most fields — could come as early as 2026. Anthropic later told the White House it expected it in late 2026 or early 2027. The year is not over.
reading: The essay offers 2026 as the earliest date and hedges it twice — could, and there are ways it could take much longer. Five months later Anthropic's submission to the White House turned it into an expectation, late 2026 or early 2027, and credited the essay.

By October 2026 pieces of the definition are claimed — machine-found proofs, agents working for days, AI writing most of a lab's code — and the labs' own staff have asked governments to help slow the frontier. Anthropic wrote in June that it was not there yet.

evidence.quote: As our CEO Dario Amodei writes in ‘Machines of Loving Grace’, we expect powerful AI systems will emerge in late 2026 or early 2027.
We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable.
This dynamic is called recursive self-improvement, and it is starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic, as we and others have described.

predictions.open: 'As early as' is a lower bound, not a deadline. Read as a forecast it falls due at the end of 2026, and in Anthropic's later wording early in 2027: the board will score it then.

predictions.title: AIs play Diplomacy as well as human experts, by 2025
predictions.words: 2025 Another major milestone! After years of tinkering and incremental progress, AIs can now play Diplomacy as well as human experts.
predictions.short: In 'What 2026 looks like', written in 2021, Kokotajlo put AIs playing Diplomacy as well as human experts in 2025. Meta's CICERO did it in 2022. He wrote that it came faster than he expected, and less generally.
reading: On the words, it came three years early: CICERO played at the level of strong human players in an online league in 2022, and that December Kokotajlo wrote that Diplomacy had happened faster than he expected.

On what he meant — people losing to the bot even when they know it is a bot — it has not happened: he wrote that CICERO would have lost under those conditions, and in 2025 that it could not win against experts who knew it was an AI. The board scores the words.

evidence.quote: Diplomacy happened faster than I expected, though in a less generalizeable way than I expected, so whatever.

And Diplomacy has turned out to be easier than I expected, though to be clear I was imagining humans losing to the bot even after knowing they were up against a bot, which is NOT what happened with Cicero, Cicero would have lost under those conditions.
CICERO was a custom-trained diplomacy model that couldn't win against human experts if they knew it was an AI.
